author: Blänsdorf et al. (in Petzet ed.)
name_in_asr: Western Buddha (55 m); Eastern Buddha (38 m)
asr_identification: the two destroyed standing colossi in the Buddha cliff, Bamiyan, Afghanistan
evidence: AMS 14C dating (Kiel 2004, ETH Zurich 2004/2009) of 21 samples from the rubble: chaff and straw from the clay plaster, ropes and wooden pegs of the fold armature, larger anchoring beams, and one beam from cave I behind the Western Buddha. All 5th–7th c. except one post-1950 beam (Indo-Afghan restoration 1969–78). Combined: Eastern Buddha 1σ 549–579, 2σ 544–595; Western Buddha 1σ 605–633, 2σ 591–644; the Eastern c. 50 years older. Three-layer clay is part of the original modelling, not a repair. The stone core itself cannot be dated.
quote: The calibration of the average of the results for both statues…shows that the Eastern Buddha was built about 50 years…Eastern Buddha            544 to 595 AD (2 σ)…Western Buddha            591 to 644 AD (2 σ).
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani on both identifications and fixes the date of the clay finish: the 38 m Buddha was finished well before Xuanzang (c. 630); the 55 m Buddha's 1σ range ends in 633 and its 2σ range in 644, so it was most probably complete, perhaps newly so, when he came. It contradicts Tanabe's view (cited in the same table) that the colossi were unfinished in 630, and Hackin's/Rowland's 2nd–5th c. dates. Supports Kuwayama's mid-6th-c. horizon.

author: Blänsdorf, Pfeffer, Melzl (in Petzet ed.)
name_in_asr: teou-shih ('metallic stone'); Eastern Buddha; Western Buddha
asr_identification: the 38 m Eastern Buddha as Xuanzang's 鍮石 statue; the 55 m Western Buddha as the golden stone image
evidence: Examination of 276 painted clay fragments (173 Western, 103 Eastern Buddha): only pink to red, blue (ultramarine), brown and ochre; several repaintings (pink, then minium, lead white, red iron oxide on the Western Buddha's sangati; blue lining); no metal foil, gilding or painted ornament found in the samples, which are mostly garment. Earlier observers recorded gold on the Eastern Buddha's skin: Hackin (1934/39) 'remnants of gold coating' on the chin; Sengupta (1969–78) 'exposed parts of the body were painted in gold'. Pink is used in China as underpainting of gold. They read 鍮石 (teou-shih) as a metal or copper-bearing stone, used by Xuanzang also for traded goods; if Xuanzang means the two existing statues, the Western is the golden stone one and the Eastern the one 'appearing as if made of metal'. They doubt that he saw the statues himself.
quote: If Xuanzang refers…to the two existing statues, the first one, being made of stone,…with sparkling golden hues and precious ornaments, would…be the taller Western Buddha, and the other one would be…the smaller Eastern Buddha appearing as if made of metal.…So far, there is no…gilding of any kind or painted ornaments.
note: Agrees with Mizutani on which colossus is which. On the 'brass': the surviving garment fragments carry paint only, no metal sheathing, against Foucher's and Ji's metal coating; the recorded gold on the Eastern Buddha's face and skin (Hackin, Sengupta) matches Kuwayama's gold paint and would explain a metallic look. That supports the study's reading that 鍮石 describes a gilded or gold-painted clay surface, not a cast metal statue. Their doubt that Xuanzang saw Bamiyan is not argued and conflicts with the Life.

author: Petzet (ed.)
evidence: Introduction quotes Beal's Xiyu ji passage (with Beal's '12 or 13 li' for the reclining Buddha) and converts to 45–50 m, 33 m and c. 333 m; no site evidence on the town or the reclining Buddha. The volume does not discuss the reclining-Buddha monastery or the royal city.
quote: This description refers to…a standing Buddha of 45–50 m height, cut into the rock cliff,
note: Repeats Beal; nothing new for 01.37 or 01.37.02.

author: Tarzi
name_in_asr: Monastère oriental (MO); grand Buddha couché de mille pieds
asr_identification: the 'Eastern Monastery' at the foot of the Buddha cliff round the Great Stupa (GS), SE of the 38 m Buddha's niche, Bamiyan, Afghanistan (or, he allows, near Gholghola where the Japanese dig)
evidence: Located in the 1970s by toponymy, topography and the one great stupa; excavated 2002–06 to find the 1000-ft reclining Buddha. Geometry: the line from the 55 m Buddha to its SW (Xuanzang's starting point PP in the royal city) is cut by a line from the GS at 2–3 li, matching 城東二三里. A slight rise in the debris fans at the GS suggested a large buried building parallel to the cliff. Excavated: caitya CH I (cruciform, round stupa 2) and CH II (stupa 4), galleries incl. A9 with clay modelling; GS faced with limestone, burnt layer with copper/bronze sheet. Chronology: first period from the Kushans (three-arched-hill coin 2nd–3rd c., Kushan bowls), stupa 2 and A9 4th–5th c., GS late 5th–early 6th c.; destruction (Sasanian or Hephthalite) and abandonment; second period from the second half of the 6th c.; burnt by Ya'qub b. Layth, 871. Reclining Buddha not found by 2006.
quote: Reste à savoir si c’est dans ce monastère (MO) que…nous devrions exhumer les restes monumentaux du Buddha couché…de mille pieds ou dans le site près de la ville de Ġolġola où fouillent…les collègues japonais. L’avenir nous le dira.
note: Supports the study's second alternative (Foucher's eastern end of the cliff) with a fuller account of the excavated monastery and its dating; Tarzi himself leaves open MO vs a site near Gholghola. He follows Foucher in putting the 先王's monastery (MR) under the scree midway between the two colossi, i.e. Kuwayama's candidate, but treats the reclining image as in a different monastery. Nothing excavated by 2006 names the monastery or shows the reclining image; the c. 19 m reclining Buddha reported from MO in 2008 is not in this paper. Place stays open.

author: Tarzi
asr_identification: the pre-Islamic royal city at the foot of the cliff W of the 55 m Buddha, partly rock-cut and partly built, extending E–W and also S of the cliff; Xuanzang's point of departure SW of the 55 m Buddha, Bamiyan, Afghanistan
evidence: From Xuanzang's 王城東北 for the 55 m Buddha: the city lay W and SW of it. VR 1 (c. ten 4 m squares, an old caravanserai W of the bazaar destroyed in the civil war): transition from cave dwellings to built houses; pre-Islamic 'Turkish' pottery (6th–9th c.), then Samanid/Ghaznavid, then Ghurid (corner of a fortification, potter's workshop). VR 2 at Sorx Qol, W of the 55 m niche at the foot of the cliff, aimed at the pre-Islamic rampart: buildings extra muros against it (a glass-makers' workshop), from the late Turkish to the end of the Ghurid period. The Ghurid capital (1155–1221) ran from the airport to Tape Almas, with Gholghola as its citadel.
quote: d’après Xuanzang, il est question d’une ville royale ou d’une grande…capitale adossée à la montagne à l’ouest de la statue du grand Buddha…de 55 m…L’emplacement de ce chantier à l’ouest de la niche du Buddha de…55 m au lieu dit Sorx Qol, pratiquement au pied de la grande falaise,…avait été choisi dans l’espoir d’y retrouver le rempart de la ville royale
note: Agrees with Foucher's town SW of the colossi and with the study's reading of 王城東北, against Kuwayama's 'nothing there worth a capital': Tarzi reports a rampart W of the 55 m niche with built-up occupation beginning in the pre-Islamic 'Turkish' period. But the rampart itself is not dated in this paper and the excavated levels are late Turkish to Ghurid, so the 630 city is not demonstrated; Ghulghula is the Ghurid citadel. The capital's site remains open, with Tarzi's evidence favouring W/SW of the 55 m Buddha.

author: Tarzi
name_in_asr: Buddha de 55 m; Buddha de 38 m (Śākyamuni, en t’eou-che)
asr_identification: the 55 m Buddha = Xuanzang's stone image NE of the royal city; the 38 m Buddha = the 鍮石 Śākyamuni
evidence: Reads Pelliot's translation: the 55 m Buddha 'répond parfaitement'; the 38 m Buddha 'très vraisemblablement' the t'eou-che Śākyamuni, its surface disputed. Dates the second great period of Bamiyan, with the 55 m Buddha, the seated Buddha of group H and most MO monuments, from the second half of the 6th c., the 55 m date 'vérifiée par l'analyse au carbone 14' of the German team; the end of the period marked by a restoration of the 38 m Buddha.
quote: Dans ce récit, ce qui est à cent pour cent sûr, la statue du Buddha…de 55 m, répond parfaitement à la description de Xuanzang.
note: Agrees with Mizutani and the study on both colossi. Note that he puts the 55 m Buddha in the second half of the 6th c. and treats the 38 m as later restored, while the ICOMOS AMS dates (petzet2009:1) make the 38 m Buddha the older (544–595) and the 55 m the later (591–644).
